en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Buddha’s Teaching on the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to Feed a Starving Tiger and the Subsequent Erection of a Stūpa,
translated by the Śramaṇa Fa-sheng of Gaochang during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Gandhāra, staying at the great city of Vaiśravaṇapura. Beneath the shade of a rocky cliff to the north of the city, he taught and transformed the Dharma for kings, ministers, and commoners, as well as the eight classes of devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans, delivering countless beings.

When his teaching was nearly complete, the Buddha smiled, and from his mouth issued fragrant light; the light was of nine colors and shone everywhere throughout all lands, and the fragrance diffused in the same manner.
At that time, the great assembly, beholding the light and smelling the fragrance, all rejoiced greatly.
Then the radiance circled the Buddha seven times and re-entered through his mouth.
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now, World-Honored One, the manifestation of these rare and auspicious signs must surely have a cause and condition; they will bring great benefit, and sentient beings shall receive your protection."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the causes and conditions for this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“As you have said, every sign manifested by the secret mouth of the Buddhas has a great cause and condition. Do you wish to hear it?”
Ānanda said:
“Yes! Indeed, O God among Gods!”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Nine kalpas ago, there was no Buddha in the world.
There was a great kingdom named Gandhamāda; the king’s name was Gandhaśrī, his queen’s name was Kṣemamukhā, and the crown prince’s name was Candanamati."
That country was vast and expansive, prosperous, joyful, and teeming with people; the lifespan of its inhabitants was fifteen hundred years.

The crown prince possessed great merit and virtue, and the world was at peace; there were no thieves or bandits, and the people were harmonious and compliant, never contending or warring against one another.

The Crown Prince was compassionate and benevolent, intelligent and wise; he had thoroughly mastered the various scriptures as well as the ninety-six kinds of paths and arts, and there was nothing regarding dignified deportment that he did not fully comprehend.
From his youth, he had always delighted in practicing charity, never begrudging the sacrifice of his body, life, or wealth.

He nurtured all living beings with a love greater than for an infant, encompassing them all with great compassion in equal measure without distinction, and he served his parents with filial piety, performing every ritual requirement with complete propriety.
"At that time, the father-king, for the sake of the crown prince, constructed a park and villa not far from the city.
That park was eight *yojanas* in length and breadth on each side; it was planted with flowers and fruits, and filled with rare and extraordinary birds, pure and magnificent.

Everywhere there were flowing springs and bathing ponds, within which there were always *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as various other species of red and white lotuses."
Peacocks, cranes, cormorants, and mandarin ducks frolic therein; it is cool, fragrant, pure, and supremely sublime.

At that time, the Prince, accompanied by his ministers, officials, queens, and court ladies, proceeded with an entourage before and behind to the garden for recreation. After seven days had passed, he turned his carriage and returned to the palace.

"At that time, those who were poor, destitute, solitary, aged, or afflicted by the hundred ailments within the realm, hearing that the Prince had returned, all came to the side of the road and held out their hands toward him."
Upon seeing this, the Prince immediately gave away his bodily ornaments, garments, gold coins, silver coins, carriages, elephants, and horses as alms;
yet when he reached the city gate, he had no further possessions remaining, and since the poor were still many, he regretted that his charity was not sufficient for all.
The Crown Prince returned to the palace; thinking of the poor people, he was so consumed by grief that he could not eat.
The King asked the Crown Prince, "Why are you so resentful?"
The Prince replied:

"Recently, while out on an excursion, I saw many poor people huddled by the roadside begging for what they lacked; I gave them whatever I had, yet it was still not sufficient, and that is why I am sorrowful."
"I now wish to request from Your Majesty the treasures of the inner treasury to provide for all under heaven; I do not know whether Your Majesty will grant this wish.
The King said, "The state treasuries are maintained for emergencies; it is not appropriate to use them for private purposes."
"Thus, the Prince's wish was not fulfilled, and his grief became twice as great as before.
A minister by the name of Jayanta, who attended upon the Prince, saw that he was fasting and was overcome with sorrow and distress."
Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Prince, saying:
"I have ten thousand gold coins which I offer to the Great God for his use as he pleases; may you not worry about poverty, and may your food and drink remain as before.
Should the money prove insufficient, I shall sell myself to provide for the Great God."
Thereupon, Jayā immediately offered ten thousand gold coins to the Prince.
The Prince sent men to take the money out of the city to give as alms to the poor; yet even after exhausting the ten thousand coins, they were still not able to reach everyone.
He returned and reported to the Prince:
"The gold and money are already exhausted, yet the poor are still many.

Thereupon, the Prince ordered an attendant official to inventory his private storehouse; they obtained another ten thousand pieces of gold and money, which he bestowed upon the poor, yet even then they were not fully satisfied.
The Prince thought to himself:
"The suffering of all people arises from poverty and the pain of being unable to obtain what they seek.
Now I shall sell my own beloved body to rescue others from their suffering and enable them to attain peace and happiness."
Having reflected thus, he cast off his precious robes and put on ordinary, worn-out garments; silently departing from the palace city, he went to another land named Vaidiśa.
There he sold himself to a brāhmaṇa for a thousand pieces of gold, which he then gave as alms to the poor.
At that time, the Brahmin sent his servant with a cart into the mountains to cut firewood to sell in the market;
after a long period had passed, he went back to gather more wood and discovered in the mountains a single piece of ox-head sandalwood weighing one hundred *jin*.
At that time, the king had suffered from leprosy since his youth, which neither medical prescriptions nor incantations could cure.
The king then said in anger,
"What is the use of a physician?"
"Every human ailment has a medicine that counteracts it; why alone should this illness of mine not receive such treatment?
He then ordered that all the physicians be executed by beheading in the marketplace.
At that time, there was a physician who prostrated himself before the king and said:
"The medicine to counteract this illness of the king's is rare in this world; though its name exists, it has never been seen."
The king asked,
"What is the name of this medicine?
He replied:
"It is called ox-head sandalwood.
The king said, "The karmic actions of men and women differ regarding their merit and transgression; there may well be a person of merit who possesses this medicine."
He immediately issued a proclamation throughout the land: "Whoever possesses this medicine shall be granted half the kingdom in exchange for it.
At that time, the Brahmin called his slave and said to him:
"Although you have earned some small profit from selling firewood since you began, it does not compare to the benefit of wealth and honor you shall now obtain."
"The King is ill; he has now offered half his kingdom to purchase ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
You should take this sandalwood and present it to the Great King; you will surely obtain your heart's desire, and I shall share this joy with you."
At that time, the slave immediately took the ox-head sandalwood and presented it to the king.
Once the king had received it, he ground it and applied it to his body; his leprosy was instantly healed.

The King was greatly rejoiced, and the ministers and citizens throughout the realm each received his blessings and reliance. He immediately summoned his officials and held a grand assembly, pardoned those in prison, bestowed alms upon the poor and destitute, and ensured harmony and joy between the high and the low.

The king commanded his great ministers to divide the palace in half, as well as all the subjects under his rule, gold, silver, precious jewels, wealth, grain, silk, slaves, carriages, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—all were divided equally.

With a hundred magnificent jeweled chariots and a thousand cavalrymen, accompanied by musicians performing songs and dances, and carrying incense, flowers, banners, and food and drink of a hundred flavors, they welcomed the slave back to the kingdom.
The king then invited him to sit together upon a precious couch, providing music, song, food, and drink for their entertainment.
The king asked the slave:
"I observe that your merit and majestic appearance are extraordinary compared to those of the world; by what cause do you dwell in such lowliness? I wish to hear your resolve."
The slave said: "Excellent!
If you wish to hear it, I shall now explain it."
"As you suspect, I was originally not a slave.
Have you perhaps heard that King Gandhamādana had a crown prince named Candanamādana who delighted in practicing charity?"
He replied,
"I have heard of it many times, but I have not yet seen it. He said:
"It is I. When the king heard this, his reverence increased all the more, and he said,
"By what cause has this come to pass?"
The Prince said:

"I am fond of practicing giving, yet even if I were to exhaust all the wealth and goods of the kingdom, it would not suffice for everyone's needs; those in poverty remain many. Since my original vow cannot be fulfilled, I have therefore abandoned the kingdom and sold my own body."
The King said, "A person's past deeds receive their retribution according to karma: practicing goodness brings joy, while committing evil brings suffering.
This was not done by you, nor was it bestowed upon you by your parents; why then have you brought disgrace upon the great expectations of the state and placed yourselves in such peril and hardship?"
"Such a thing as this is rare in the world; there must be some extraordinary insight behind it. I pray you, explain its meaning.
The Prince replied, "I originally resolved my mind to vow to deliver all living beings, practicing the various pāramitās and aspiring for Bodhi."
The king said: "Excellent!
I greatly rejoice."
The Prince said to the King, "I now return the kingdom to you; I only seek one wish, provided it may not be denied.
He replied:
"What is your wish? the Prince asked.

He replied, "I wish to take the wealth and treasures from the central treasury to provide for the poor, the orphaned and elderly, the weak and infirm, and those suffering from a hundred ailments throughout the world; I shall give as freely as I desire for fifty full days, and I share the merit therein with you."
The King said: "Excellent!
As for wealth and property, you may employ them as you see fit. As for this reward of half a kingdom, it is your rightful share for your merit; I dare not accept it."
The Prince said:
"Excellent!
You bestow wealth upon me; I shall offer my kingdom to you."
"I am fond of practicing charity, whereas your kingdom delights in pleasure; our people have different natures and our aspirations are not the same.
The King said, "This practice is vast and profound; it is beyond my reach."
"When you attain the Way, I pray that you will deliver me.
Thereupon, the Prince dispatched messengers to proclaim to all the kingdoms: "If there are those who are poor, orphaned, aged, or infirm, let them all come to the assembly."

At that time, the Prince ordered his attendants to open all the treasuries and transport the wealth to level ground; he bestowed it upon the poor for fifty full days, such that those who were impoverished became wealthy, and there was none who did not rejoice.
"At that time, after the Prince had abdicated his kingdom and departed, the ministers were struck with alarm and wept aloud, saying to the King:
'Last night the Prince suddenly vanished; we know not where he is.'"
Upon hearing these words, the king fell from his couch, losing consciousness and unable to recognize those around him.

The queen, the ladies of the inner court, the concubines, as well as the ministers, officials, and commoners, were all struck with wonder and alarm; overcome with grief and distress, they raised their voices in lamentation and rushed out in all directions to search for the prince.

At that time, the King’s consort, fearing she would lose her crown prince, became distraught as if mad; she immediately fled from the city with the other queens and consorts, disrobing their lower garments and letting down their hair, running hither and thither in pursuit to search for the prince.

Fearing that the Queen might die from the anguish of longing for her son, the King immediately prepared his carriage with his ministers and departed the city to search for the Queen and seek news of the Prince.

Ten *li* from the capital, amidst the grasses of a desolate marsh, he saw the lady followed by several palace attendants, beating their breasts and weeping; her hair was disheveled and her eyes swollen as she pushed through the thickets of wild plants, searching for the Prince.
When the king saw this, his grief intensified further.
He stepped forward, took the lady’s hand, and with tears streaming down his face, he exhorted her, saying:

"My son possessed merit and virtue; he was compassionate, filial, and generous, giving things away without resentment. Even after exhausting his wealth and treasures in alms to the whole world, he still felt insufficient; he constantly harbored regret that he had nothing left to bestow."
"My son, you must now depart in secret; you will surely seek wealth in another land to practice charity, or perhaps sell yourself to provide for the poor.
For now, let us return together to the palace; do not grieve so greatly."
"I shall now dispatch messengers to various kingdoms to inquire after news; I will surely bring my son back.
The lady rebuked him, saying, "It is because you, O King, are stingy and greedy, cherishing wealth while failing to love and care for your son."
"Now, can wealth truly be considered one's own body?
The king said, "My error was in the past; what use is regret now?"
"Let us return to the palace together for now to ensure we do not lose our son.
I shall now go forth in person in all directions to search for him, and I will certainly bring my son back.
The lady shed tears and said:
"Now that I have lost my son, what is the use of living?
I would rather die here than return empty-handed.

When I observed my son’s body, I saw he was unaware of hunger or thirst; though he suffered the pains of illness, he did not regard them as a calamity. Now that I return to this emptiness, upon what can I rely?"

Thereupon, the Crown Prince’s consort and concubines disheveled their hair and disarrayed their heads; they cried out to Heaven and struck the earth, looking in all four directions but not seeing the Crown Prince.
Wailing to Heaven and bowing their heads, they spoke while drinking in their tears:
“Heaven, Earth, Sun, Moon, Parents, and tutelary deities!
"If I have committed any transgressions, I now repent them all; I pray that you, my lord, may soon meet with me.
Thereupon, the king forcibly led the lady, the crown prince, and the queen back to the palace in a carriage.

"At that time, while the Prince was far away in another country, his two eyes, hands, and feet twitched three times; his heart was filled with sorrow and fear as if he had forgotten something, and he immediately took leave of that king to return to his own country."
The King ordered his attendants to prepare one hundred ornate jeweled chariots, a thousand cavalrymen, ten thousand gold coins, and one hundred thousand silver coins.
The King had five hundred ministers, each of whom presented ten thousand gold coins and one hundred thousand silver coins as gifts to escort the Prince.

The king, together with ten million ministers, escorted the crown prince to the border of his own kingdom; having arranged a great assembly and expressed their mutual thanks with joy, they then departed from one another.
The Prince reflected:
"Since my youth, my feet have never moved in vain, nor have my eyes ever looked aimlessly.

When I previously left the country, I did not take leave of my parents; it must be that my parents and the ministers and people of the kingdom are grieving and distressed because they fear losing me."
"I must now depart quickly to let them know the news.
He further reflected:
"The road is vast and far; it cannot be reached in haste."
"I fear that my parents, out of deep affection and longing, might even lose their lives; what means should I employ to ensure that news reaches them quickly?
At that time, there was a crow that was skilled at speaking human language, who addressed the Prince, saying:
"Your benevolence and virtue are most profound, and your grace extends everywhere; why worry that this cannot be accomplished?"
"What do you wish to accomplish? I shall assist you.
The Prince replied, "I wish to entrust you with one matter; I hope you will not refuse it."
The crow said,
“I obey your command!
The Prince said:
"I beg you to deliver this letter to my father, the King.
The crow said, "You must act with haste; now is precisely the right time."
The Prince wrote a letter and gave it to the crow; the crow took the letter in its beak and flew to his native country, placing the letter before the King.
The King opened and read the letter, learning news of his son, and was filled with great joy; he immediately rose and entered the palace.
He said to the lady, "As I have told you, know that you shall not lose your son; within a few days you will surely see him.
Upon hearing this, the lady was as if returning to life from death; she clapped her hands and exclaimed in praise:
"May all under heaven be peaceful and happy, may they obtain all their wishes, and may their lifespans be immeasurable!
At that time, the ministers, noble families, men and women, and the old and young throughout the kingdom, hearing that the Prince had returned, all cried out, "Ten thousand years!"
The King, together with several tens of millions of ministers, prepared his carriage and led a procession to go out and welcome the Prince.
As they met on the road, the Prince saw his father; he immediately descended from his precious chariot, went forward to clasp his father’s feet in salutation, and addressed the King, saying:
"In my conduct as a son, I have been unfilial, causing Your Majesty to humble yourself and bringing alarm to the entire realm. I pray you will graciously grant me your forgiveness!"
The King said, "Excellent!

Father and son met, their hearts filled with a mingling of sorrow and joy; they turned their carriage back toward the palace, and among all the people and commoners of the kingdom, there was none who did not rejoice.
Beggars from distant lands, hearing that the Crown Prince had returned and that they would receive much wealth, all came from afar to beg from him.

The Crown Prince sent men to carry loads of money and goods to a level open space at the head of the main road to distribute to the poor; for an entire year, this was done daily without ceasing, so that those who came from the four quarters all obtained what they desired.
At that time, the father king spoke to the crown prince together with his various ministers, saying:
"From this day forward, regarding the treasures and jewels in the royal treasury, you may use them as you require; do not harbor any doubts or hesitation."
"The virtue of giving is esteemed far and wide; even when enemies and wicked people hear of the Prince's meritorious deeds, they will naturally cultivate goodness.

At that time, there was a divine seer and master of the five supernatural powers named Courageous (Vīra), who, together with five hundred disciples, was practicing meditation and cultivating the Way within a great rocky cave on this mountain. He sought Bodhi with his whole being, desiring to deliver all from suffering and to transform the world so that all might practice goodness.
At that time, Prince Candramati took various kinds of food and drink of a hundred flavors and ascended the mountain to make offerings to the sages and practitioners.
Then, the master sage offered prayers for the prince and preached the Dharma for him.

The Crown Prince’s heart was filled with joy, and his mind delighted in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); he had no desire to return to his kingdom. He regarded his palace as a place of birth in hell, viewed his wife, children, and kinsmen as shackles and fetters, and perceived the pleasures of the five desires as the torments of hell.

Having reflected thus, he immediately removed his jeweled necklace, his fine garments, and all his carriages, horses, and attendants, entrusting them to his subordinate ministers and dispatching them back to his kingdom.
Thereupon, the Prince donned a deer-skin garment and remained in the mountains to study the Way under his teacher, diligently seeking out spiritual arts.
At that time, the Prince’s attendant returned to the kingdom and informed the King:
"The Prince has gone up the mountain to serve an immortal; he remains there to study the Way and is unwilling to return to the palace."
"I shall master all the scriptures and incantations, and I vow to attain the stage of non-returning.
The King said,
"How bitter this is!"
When people of the world obtain a son, they attain joy and happiness; they rely on him in their old age to benefit the state and eliminate calamities.
I, however, having obtained this son, constantly harbor sorrow and suffering; I do not desire wealth or nobility, nor do I seek intimacy with my kin.
"In one so afflicted as this, what path could there possibly be?
He immediately summoned his ministers to deliberate on this matter, and the ministers said, "The Crown Prince loves the Way;
he does not covet worldly glory, for his heart’s desire is the Unconditioned."
"Since he has not returned to the kingdom, what can be done?
Your Majesty should dispatch an envoy to ascertain his intent; if he truly will not return, you must deliberate upon what is appropriate.
The King immediately dispatched an envoy to inquire of the Prince:
"I now wait for you as one parched with thirst longs for a drink; what is the meaning of your lingering in the mountains without returning?
Now the lady, the queen, and the concubines wave their tears and gaze down the road, wailing and lamenting, unable to control themselves."
"The Master values the security of his parents; it would not be right for him to suffer such hardship or opposition.
If you comply with his request, he will surely return!
The messenger received the command, and the instructions were as stated.
The Crown Prince replied:

"All things are impermanent; physical forms do not endure for long. The joy of family life turns to suffering upon separation; one's destiny is determined by heaven and cannot be controlled by oneself."
When impermanence arrives, even father and son cannot save one another.
Now, seeking the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and desiring to deliver all from suffering, I shall first deliver my parents on the day I attain the Way.
"This place is not far away, and I should go there at once to pay my respects.
My resolve is already settled; Your Majesty should instead devise a plan to continue the line of succession for the kingdom.
Returning with this message, he informed the king in detail of the aforementioned matters.
The King immediately summoned his assembled ministers and established another as the Crown Prince.

At that time, the King’s consort, along with the Crown Prince’s queen, ladies-in-waiting, and attendants, took with them the Crown Prince’s garments and articles for personal adornment, as well as various sweet fruits, food and drink, incense and flowers, and musical instruments. With these leading and following them before and behind, they ascended the mountain to the place where the Crown Prince was, and provided a meal for the assembly of sages.
Upon welcoming the Crown Prince, the lady said:
"One plants grain to prevent hunger, digs wells for times of thirst, builds city walls to ward off thieves, and raises children to serve one in old age."
"If you do not return to the kingdom now, my life will not be preserved.
The Prince knelt upright and said to the Lady,
"To leave home and dwell in the mountains, changing one's form and altering one's dress, is like spittle falling from the mouth— it is no longer fit for consumption."
"A recluse who dwells in seclusion contributes nothing to the state.
Since our principles and divisions are already settled, they cannot be altered; I would rather let my body be crushed here than ever return."
"I pray that you, Mother, will return soon, so that I may immediately go to visit you.

Thereupon, the lady, the Crown Prince, and the Queen Consort, seeing that the Prince’s resolve was firm and that he had no intention of returning, wept with grief and distress as they returned along the road.

At that time, the king, hoping only for the return of his consort with the crown prince, went out of the city with his ministers to welcome them; he saw only his consort and the queen of the crown prince with their hair disheveled and unkempt, beating their breasts and wailing as they returned empty-handed along the road.
The King became even more distressed; the assembled ministers and the multitude of people all wept with tears as he turned his carriage back toward the palace.
Thereupon, the King offered words of apology to the Queen and the Prince’s wife, saying:
"My son’s fondness for the Way is something rarely found in this world."
Nurturing with compassion and providing universal relief, there are none who do not receive his grace.
He is a treasure of this land, no ordinary vessel.
Now he delights in dwelling in the mountains to cultivate his aspirations; simply ensure that he remains safe and at peace, and we shall meet again from time to time.
"Now, as we are not far from each other, I shall send you food and drink and maintain correspondence so that you may find some comfort.
Thereupon, having received the King's consolation, the lady’s grief subsided slightly.
From time to time, he sent people carrying food and drink, various sweet fruits, and all kinds of delicious delicacies to the mountains to make offerings to the Prince.
Thus it continued for many years; the Prince also occasionally came down to inquire after his parents, before returning once more to the mountains to cultivate the Way.
At the foot of that mountain was a precipitous cliff and a deep valley, at the bottom of which lived a tigress who had recently given birth to seven cubs.

At that time, a great snowfall fell; the tigress had been nursing her cubs for many days without being able to seek food, yet she remained there guarding them from hunger, fearing they would freeze to death.
The snow fell incessantly, and the mother and cub were so famished and exhausted that their lives would not last much longer.
Driven by the fires of hunger, the tigress was about to devour her own offspring.
At that time, the various seers and practitioners on the mountain witnessed this event and exhorted one another, saying:
"Who can sacrifice their own body to rescue and deliver sentient beings? Now is precisely the right time.
Having heard this, the Prince proclaimed:
"Excellent!"
“My wish has been fulfilled!

He went to the edge of the cliff and looked down; seeing the mother tiger with her cubs covered by the snow, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion. Standing still upon the mountain peak, he entered meditative absorption in silence and immediately attained the pure *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
He beheld the events of countless past kalpas, and likewise those of the future.
He immediately returned and informed his teacher and five hundred fellow students, saying:
"I shall now sacrifice my body; I pray that you will each rejoice in this.
His teacher said:
"I have studied the Way for but a short time and my knowledge and vision are not yet broad; why do you suddenly end your life and abandon this cherished body?
The Prince replied, "I once made a vow that I should sacrifice a thousand bodies."
"In the past, I have already sacrificed nine hundred and ninety-nine bodies; today, what I sacrifice completes the full thousand.
For this reason, I offer my body; I pray that the Master will rejoice in this."
The Master said:
"Your aspirations are lofty and sublime; none can equal them.
You shall surely attain the Way first; do not forget to include me."
The Prince took his leave of his teacher and departed.
Thereupon, the Great Master and five hundred seers and adepts, their eyes filled with tears, escorted the Prince as far as the edge of a mountain cliff.
At that time, the elder Pūraṇa, accompanied by five hundred men and women, brought food and drink up the mountain to make offerings;
seeing the Prince sacrifice his body, he was moved with grief and wept, following the Prince to the edge of the mountain cliff.
"Then, before the great multitude, the Prince made this great vow:

'By the merit of my sacrifice of this body to save the lives of these beings, may I swiftly attain Bodhi; may I obtain the adamantine body, the unconditioned Dharma-body of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and may I cause those who have not crossed over to cross over, those who have not been liberated to be liberated, and those who have not found peace to find peace.'"
This body of mine is impermanent, a collection of suffering, affliction, and manifold poisons.
It is impure, with its nine orifices constantly overflowing; it is stung by the four great venomous serpents of the elements and pursued and harmed by the five bandits with drawn swords.

Such a body is ungrateful; though one provides it with fine delicacies, exquisite flavors, and the pleasures of the five desires, after its life comes to an end, it offers no reward of merit in gratitude, but instead falls into hell to undergo immeasurable suffering.
"The human body should only be made to suffer; it must not be granted pleasure.
Having thus rebuked his own body for its various faults in many ways, the Prince further made this vow:
"Now, with my flesh and blood, I shall save that starving tigress."

As for my remaining bone relics, my parents will later surely erect a stupa for them. Should any sentient beings suffer from various physical ailments or the karmic consequences of past offenses such that they cannot be cured by decoctions, medicines, acupuncture, or moxibustion, if they come to my stupa and make offerings with a sincere heart, their illnesses—regardless of their severity—will surely be healed within no more than one hundred days.
"If this be true and not false, may the devas rain down fragrant flowers.
As soon as he spoke, the devas rained down *mandārava* flowers, and the earth trembled everywhere.
The Prince then removed his deerskin garment to wrap around his head and eyes; with palms joined, he threw himself before the tiger.
Thereupon, the tigress mother obtained the Bodhisattva’s flesh, and both mother and son were restored to life.

At that time, the people on the cliff edge looked down and saw the Prince being devoured by the tiger; his bones and flesh were strewn in disarray. They wailed and cried out so loudly that the sound shook the mountains.
Some beat their breasts and threw themselves to the ground, rolling about in agony; some entered into meditative contemplation; and some prostrated themselves, repenting before the Prince.

"At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, as well as Śakra, Lord of Devas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and tens of millions of sun and moon deities, all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed bodhi. They performed music and dance, burned incense, scattered flowers, and offered *mandārava* blossoms to the Prince, proclaiming these words:
'Excellent!'"
"O Mahāsattva! Before long from now, you shall sit at the site of enlightenment.
Having thus proclaimed this three times, they each returned to their celestial palaces.
The five hundred seers all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and the Great Master of Seers attained the patience of non-arising.
On the following day, the king and his consort dispatched messengers carrying food and drink to go up the mountain to provide sustenance for the Prince.

Upon arriving at the permanent stone grotto, he saw only bedding, deerskin garments, a parasol, an alms bowl, a mendicant’s staff, a water flask, and a washbasin—all within the chamber—but the Prince was nowhere to be seen.
He questioned everyone everywhere, but no one responded; he saw only groups of five or ten sages facing one another, weeping.
Upon reaching the master’s dwelling, he found only the sage master sitting with his cheek propped in his hand, his eyes filled with tears as he groaned.
They questioned him from all sides, but he offered no response.
Terrified, the messenger immediately provided food and drink to the various rishis and fled back to report the matter in detail to the lady.
The lady said, "I have not seen my son; have you seen any of the seers?
He replied:
"However, I see the seers, ten by ten and five by five, facing one another and weeping.
The lady said, "How tragic!"
"My son is dead!
he cried, beating his breast and shouting as he rushed to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king fell from his bed, losing consciousness and becoming unaware of those around him.
The ministers and the multitude gathered at the king’s side, prostrating themselves and remonstrating, saying:
"We do not know whether the prince is truly in the mountains or not; why do you grieve so bitterly?
We pray that Your Majesty will rest for a while!"
Thereupon, the king, along with his consort, the ladies of the harem, the court attendants, ministers, officials, and commoners, lifted their robes and went barefoot, rushing up the mountain.
At that time, the elder Pūraṇa also came forward to inform the king, saying:
"Yesterday, the prince threw himself down from the cliff to feed his flesh to the tigers; now only his bones remain scattered upon the ground."
Thereupon, the elder led the king to the place where the crown prince’s corpse lay.
The king, along with his consort, the queens, the court ladies, the ministers, and the officials and commoners, raised their voices in lamentation, causing the mountains and valleys to tremble.
The King and the Queen prostrated themselves over the Prince’s corpse; their hearts and livers were as if severed, and they fainted, losing consciousness.
The Consort leaned forward to support his head and arrange the Prince’s hair; her heart and liver were crushed with grief, and she wailed with a piercing cry, saying, "How thin is my fate!
To lose my honored one while he is still alive!"
"Today he is gone forever; I shall never see him again.
It would be better for my own body to be crushed into dust than for my lord to perish so suddenly.
Now that the Prince is dead, what use is life to me?"
At that time, the ministers said to the king:
"The Crown Prince has vowed to bestow gifts in order to deliver all living beings; he cannot escape the assault and seizure of the demon of impermanence.
Before his body becomes putrid and rotten, it is fitting that you provide offerings."

He immediately gathered the remains and brought them out from the mouth of the mountain valley. On level ground, he piled up sandalwood fuel and various kinds of fragrant wood, along with all manner of perfumes, ghee, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, to perform the cremation of the Prince.
Having collected the relics, he placed them in precious vessels and erected a stupa made of the seven treasures there, adorning it with all sorts of precious objects.
The four sides of that stupa were ten li in length and breadth, arrayed with various flowers and fruits, flowing springs, and bathing pools that were majestic, pure, and clean.
The king constantly commanded performers of the four types of music to provide offerings day and night, providing entertainment for this stupa.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The crown prince at that time was myself;
the father-king at that time was my current father, King Śuddhodana."
The lady at that time was Queen Māyā;
the consort at that time is now Gopī;
and the minister Jayasena was Ānanda.
At that time, the great master of the mountain seers was Maitreya;
King Pārśva was Nanda; and the brahmin of that time was Rāhula.

Since time immemorial, Maitreya Bodhisattva has always been my teacher; yet because I practiced giving without sparing even my own body or life to save sentient beings, I have surpassed him by nine kalpas and have now attained Buddhahood to provide infinite salvation.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, eighty-four thousand devas, nāgas, and humans all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, impartial mind of the Way; eight thousand bhikṣus, having exhausted their outflows and untied their fetters, attained the path of arhatship.
When the king, along with his ministers, devas, nāgas, and spirits, heard what the Buddha had said, they were all greatly rejoiced; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.

In the original chronicle of the Dan region, it is recorded that at that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the king immediately erected a great stūpa at that very spot, named "The Stūpa of the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice to the Starving Tiger," which remains extant to this day.

On the mountain slope to the east of the stupa, there were monastic quarters, lecture halls, and viharas, where there were always five thousand monks and the four requisites for their support were abundantly provided.

At that time, people from various countries suffering from leprosy, insanity, deafness, blindness, lameness, or various other ailments would all come to this stupa to burn incense, light lamps, smear the ground with fragrant mud, sweep and sprinkle it clean, and prostrate themselves in repentance; thus, all their hundred maladies were healed.
Those sent previously would depart, and those who arrived later would likewise do so;
there were always more than a hundred people, and regardless of their status—whether noble or humble—they all behaved in this manner, never ceasing for a moment.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Buddha’s Teaching on the Bodhisattva Casting Himself to Feed a Starving Tiger and the Subsequent Erection of a Stūpa.
